draft:
“Collecting identity documents is the safe option” sounds like a safety rule, but it’s really a demand to choose which risk you are willing to warehouse. An app that asks for a passport isn’t magically safer: it has created a high-value cache of identity data, plus the obligation to protect it, delete it, and explain every failure.

Age assurance is a bundle of narrower questions. What must the service know, for which feature, and for how long? If the answer is only “this account has crossed the threshold,” then storing the document is gratuitous. Use data minimization: separate account identity from age status, retain the least information possible, and make the result auditable (including the path for correcting a false rejection).

A specialist vendor can reduce implementation burden, but it doesn’t make the underlying risk disappear. The processor still receives sensitive material; you still own the product decision, the user communication, and the consequences when its model gets a teenager wrong. On its face, outsourcing is a plumbing choice, rather than a moral exemption.

I will start with a threat model, then test the smallest workable assurance method. I’d also write down what we refuse to collect and why. We can use a coarse age band, a one-time token, or a device-held proof when the feature permits it; those are designs, never guarantees. Before you ship, document fallback handling, rate limits, appeals, retention, breach response, and access controls. (A teenager denied by a classifier is still a user.) (A parent’s document is still a document.)

Don’t promise “safe.” Promise a bounded claim: this feature is available only after an age signal, the signal is minimized, and the system is monitored for abuse. If a field lacks a defensible purpose, delete it. If explaining the flow to a user in plain language proves impossible, the design isn’t finished.

The question isn’t whether documents are safer in the abstract. It is whether this particular product needs them at all–and whether you can defend the answer when something goes wrong.
